paper_id: Episodic flood inundations of the northern plains of Mars.pdf
title: Episodic flood inundations of the northern plains of Mars
authors: Fairén, Alberto G.; Dohm, James M.; Baker, Victor R.; De Pablo, Miguel A.; Ruiz, Javier; Ferris, Justin C.; Anderson, Robert C.
file_name: Episodic flood inundations of the northern plains of Mars.pdf
research_region: Northern plains of Mars; Tharsis region; Chryse Planitia; Elysium rise
data_instruments_samples: Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) topographic data; geologic and geomorphic mapping; stratigraphic analysis; hydrologic and paleotopographic reconstructions; Viking and Mars Orbiter Camera (MOC) images; literature synthesis of outflow channel and valley network data
abstract_note: Throughout the recorded history of Mars, liquid water has distinctly shaped its landscape, including the prominent circum-Chryse and the northwestern slope valleys outﬂow channel systems, and the extremely ﬂat northern plains topography at the distal reaches of these outﬂow channel systems. Paleotopographic reconstructions of the Tharsis magmatic complex reveal the existence of an Europe-sized Noachian drainage basin and subsequent aquifer system in eastern Tharsis. This basin is proposed to have sourced outburst ﬂoodwaters that sculpted the outﬂow channels, and ponded to form various hypothesized oceans, seas, and lakes episodically through time. These ﬂoodwaters decreased in volume with time due to inadequate groundwater recharge of the Tharsis aquifer system. Martian topography, as observed from the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter, corresponds well to these ancient ﬂood inundations, including the approximated shorelines that have been proposed for the northern plains. Stratigraphy, geomorphology, and topography record at least one great Noachian-Early Hesperian northern plains ocean, a Late Hesperian sea inset within the margin of the high water marks of the previous ocean, and a number of widely distributed minor lakes that may represent a reduced Late Hesperian sea, or ponded waters in the deepest reaches of the northern plains related to minor Tharsis- and Elysium-induced Amazonian ﬂooding.
research_content: This paper presents a hydrogeological model linking the episodic development of the Tharsis Magmatic Complex (TMC) and associated superplume activity to the formation of large-scale flood inundations in the northern plains of Mars. The authors reconstruct paleotopography and analyze geomorphology, stratigraphy, and topographic data, including Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) measurements, to identify evidence for a Noachian-Early Hesperian great ocean (Shoreline 1), a Late Hesperian smaller ocean or sea (Shoreline 2), and multiple minor lakes during the Amazonian. They propose that pulses of magmatic-driven tectonism and volcanism at Tharsis and Elysium triggered outburst floods that sculpted outflow channels and ponded water to form these bodies, with volumes decreasing over time due to inadequate groundwater recharge. The study integrates geologic mapping, valley network analysis, and hydrologic modeling to support a conceptual model of episodic flood inundations shaping the northern lowlands.

screening_result.reason: This paper directly addresses episodic flood inundations in the northern plains of Mars including Chryse Planitia, discussing paleotopographic reconstructions and evidence for ponding and hypothesized oceans, seas, and lakes. It explicitly mentions the formation of a Noachian-Early Hesperian northern plains ocean and related shorelines, making it highly relevant to the question of an ancient ocean in Chryse Planitia.

paper_id: Formation and disruption of aquifers in southwestern Chryse Planitia, Mars.pdf
title: Formation and disruption of aquifers in southwestern Chryse Planitia, Mars
authors: Rodríguez, José Alexis Palmero; Tanaka, Kenneth L.; Kargel, Jeffrey S.; Dohm, James M.; Kuzmin, Ruslan; Fairén, Alberto G.; Sasaki, Sho; Komatsu, Goro; Schulze-Makuch, Dirk; Jianguo, Yan
file_name: Formation and disruption of aquifers in southwestern Chryse Planitia, Mars.pdf
data_instruments_samples: Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) digital elevation models; Mars Global Surveyor Mars Orbiter Camera (MOC) visible imagery; Mars Express High Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) imagery; Mars Odyssey Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS) daytime infrared and visible imagery
abstract_note: We present geologic evidence suggesting that after the development of Mars’ cryolithosphere, the formation of aquifers in southwestern Chryse Planitia and their subsequent disruption led to extensive regional resurfacing during the Late Hesperian, and perhaps even during the Amazonian. In our model, these aquifers formed preferentially along thrust faults associated with wrinkle ridges, as well as along fault systems peripheral to impact craters. The characteristics of degraded wrinkle ridges and impact craters in southwestern Chryse Planitia indicate a profound role of subsurface volatiles and especially liquid water in the upper crust (the upper one hundred to a few thousands of meters). Like lunar wrinkle ridges, the martian ones are presumed to mark the surface extensions of thrust faults, but in our study area the wrinkle ridges are heavily modiﬁed. Wrinkle ridges and nearby plains have locally undergone collapse, and in other areas they are associated with domical intrusions we interpret as mud volcanoes and mud diapirs. In at least one instance, a sinuous valley emanates from a modiﬁed wrinkle ridge, further indicating hydrological inﬂuences on these thrust-fault-controlled features. A key must be the formation of volatile-rich crust. Primary crustal formation and differentiation incorporated juvenile volatiles into the global crust, but the crustal record here was then strongly modiﬁed by the giant Chryse impact. The decipherable rock record here begins with the Chryse impact and continues with the resulting basin’s erosion and inﬁlling, which includes outﬂow channel activity. We propose that in Simud Vallis surface ﬂow dissection into the base of the cryolithosphere-produced zones where water inﬁltrated and migrated along SW-dipping strata deformed by the Chryse impact, thereby forming an extensive aquifer in southwestern Chryse Planitia. In this region, compressive stresses produced by the rise of Tharsis led to the formation of wrinkle ridges. Zones of high fracture density within the highly strained planes of the thrust faults underlying the wrinkle ridges formed regions of high permeability; thus, groundwater likely ﬂowed and gathered along these tectonic structures to form zones of elevated permeability. Volatile depletion and migration within the upper crustal materials, predominantly along fault systems, led to structurally controlled episodic resurfacing in southwestern Chryse Planitia. The erosional modiﬁcation of impact craters in this region is linked to these processes. This erosion is scale independent over a range of crater diameters from a few hundred meters to tens of kilometers. According to our model, pressurized water and sediment intruded and locally extruded and caused crustal subsidence and other degradational activity across this region. The modiﬁcation of craters across this wide range of sizes, according to our model, implies that there was intensive mobilization of liquid water in the upper crust ranging from about one hundred to several thousand meters deep.
research_content: This paper presents geologic evidence that after the development of Mars' cryolithosphere, aquifers formed preferentially along thrust faults associated with wrinkle ridges and along fault systems peripheral to impact craters in southwestern Chryse Planitia. The authors constructed digital elevation models using Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) data and analyzed visible imagery from Mars Global Surveyor MOC, Mars Express HRSC, and Mars Odyssey THEMIS instruments to study geomorphology and morphometry of degraded wrinkle ridges, impact craters, and plains materials. They identify three geomorphologically distinct zones of resurfacing (elevated, moderate, and low) and interpret the formation of extensive aquifers along thrust faults and impact crater fractures, which led to episodic resurfacing through groundwater emergence, subsurface erosion, collapse, thermokarst activity, mud volcanism, and sedimentary volcanism. The study concludes that these processes caused widespread degradation of plains materials, wrinkle ridges, and impact crater rims into knobs and knobby ridges, with resurfacing extending from the Late Hesperian into the Amazonian.

screening_result.reason: This paper presents geologic evidence for aquifers and extensive liquid water mobilization in southwestern Chryse Planitia, which is directly relevant to understanding the presence of ancient water bodies, potentially including an ancient ocean.

paper_id: Evidence of volcanic and glacial activity in Chryse and Acidalia Planitiae, Mars.pdf
title: Evidence of volcanic and glacial activity in Chryse and Acidalia Planitiae, Mars
authors: Martínez-Alonso, Sara; Mellon, Michael T.; Banks, Maria E.; Keszthelyi, Laszlo P.; McEwen, Alfred S.
file_name: Evidence of volcanic and glacial activity in Chryse and Acidalia Planitiae, Mars.pdf
data_instruments_samples: HiRISE images; MOLA elevation data; MOC narrow-angle images; THEMIS visible and infrared images; CTX images; CRISM spectral data; HiRISE stereo anaglyphs
abstract_note: Chryse and Acidalia Planitiae show numerous examples of enigmatic landforms previously interpreted to have been inﬂuenced by a water/ice-rich geologic history. These landforms include giant polygons bounded by kilometer-scale arcuate troughs, bright pitted mounds, and mesa-like features. To investigate the signiﬁcance of the last we have analyzed in detail the region between 60°N, 290°E and 10°N, 360°E utilizing HiRISE (High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment) images as well as regional-scale data for context. The mesas may be analogous to terrestrial tuyas (emergent sub-ice volcanoes), although deﬁnitive proof has not been identiﬁed. We also report on a blocky unit and associated landforms (drumlins, eskers, inverted valleys, kettle holes) consistent with ice-emplaced volcanic or volcano-sedimentary ﬂows. The spatial association between tuya-like mesas, ice-emplaced ﬂows, and further possible evidence of volcanism (deﬂated ﬂow fronts, volcanic vents, columnar jointing, rootless cones), and an extensive ﬂuid-rich substratum (giant polygons, bright mounds, rampart craters), allows for the possibility of glaciovolcanic activity in the region.
research_content: This paper investigates enigmatic landforms in Chryse and Acidalia Planitiae, Mars, to assess evidence of volcanic and glacial activity. The authors analyzed approximately 190 HiRISE images, along with MOLA, MOC, THEMIS, CTX, and CRISM data, focusing on mesas, blocky units, and associated landforms such as drumlins, eskers, kettles, giant polygons, bright mounds, and rampart craters. They identify mesas with central edifices resembling terrestrial tuyas, blocky units consistent with ice-emplaced volcanic or volcano-sedimentary flows, and glacial landforms indicative of past ice-sheet activity. The spatial association of these features suggests possible glaciovolcanic activity and a fluid-rich substratum in the region, implying a paleoclimate different from present conditions.

screening_result.reason: The paper discusses enigmatic landforms in Chryse Planitia that have been interpreted as influenced by water/ice-rich history, including possible glaciovolcanic activity. While it does not directly address an ancient ocean, it provides relevant geological context about water-related processes in the region.

paper_id: Fluid expulsion in terrestrial sedimentary basins_ A process providing potential analogs for giant polygons and mounds in the martian lowlands.pdf
title: Fluid expulsion in terrestrial sedimentary basins: A process providing potential analogs for giant polygons and mounds in the martian lowlands
authors: Allen, Carlton C.; Oehler, Dorothy Z.; Etiope, Giuseppe; Rensbergen, Pieter Van; Baciu, Calin; Feyzullayev, Akper; Martinelli, Giovanni; Tanaka, Kazuhiro; Rooij, David Van
file_name: Fluid expulsion in terrestrial sedimentary basins_ A process providing potential analogs for giant polygons and mounds in the martian lowlands.pdf
data_instruments_samples: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX images; HiRISE images; CRISM spectral data; Viking Mars Digital Image Model (MDIM); Mars Orbital Laser Altimeter (MOLA); Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS); terrestrial seismic data and bathymetric surveys from Gulf of Cadiz, North Sea, Norwegian margin, and other sedimentary basins; geological mapping and basin analysis
abstract_note: On Earth, burial of ﬁne-grained sediments in offshore passive margins (e.g., underwater fans and deltas) commonly results in ﬂuid expulsion features including large-scale polygonal fractures, mud volcanoes, and pockmarks. Comparison of resulting offshore polygons and mud volcanoes with giant polygons and high-albedo mounds in the Chryse–Acidalia region of Mars shows the terrestrial and martian features to be similar in size, morphology, geologic context, and general co-occurrence within the same basin. These similarities suggest that the process of terrestrial ﬂuid expulsion may provide an analog that could link the giant polygons and mounds in Chryse and Acidalia to a single process.
research_content: This paper presents the hypothesis that fluid expulsion features in terrestrial sedimentary basins, such as large-scale polygonal fractures and mud volcanoes, provide potential analogs for giant polygons and high-albedo mounds in the Chryse–Acidalia region of Mars. The authors compare terrestrial fluid-expulsion features with Martian features in terms of geologic setting, morphology, size, spatial distribution, and sedimentary processes. They analyze the spatial correlation of mounds and giant polygons in northern Chryse and southern Acidalia Planitiae using high-resolution orbital imagery (CTX and HiRISE) and spectral data from CRISM. The study finds that the Martian giant polygons and mounds share similarities with terrestrial fluid-expulsion features in size, morphology, and geologic context, suggesting a linked formation process involving sediment deposition, dewatering, and fluid escape. The authors discuss implications for the role of water and methane release in the Martian lowlands and propose that the Martian features may represent an intermediate form of fluid expulsion analogous to terrestrial mud volcanoes and polygonal fault systems.

screening_result.reason: The paper compares terrestrial fluid expulsion features with giant polygons and mounds in Chryse Planitia, suggesting processes involving fluid movement in the subsurface. This provides useful analogs and context for interpreting water-related features in the region.

paper_id: On the origin of the Vastitas Borealis Formation in Chryse and Acidalia Planitiae, Mars.pdf
title: On the origin of the Vastitas Borealis Formation in Chryse and Acidalia Planitiae, Mars
authors: Salvatore, M. R.; Christensen, P. R.
file_name: On the origin of the Vastitas Borealis Formation in Chryse and Acidalia Planitiae, Mars.pdf
data_instruments_samples: Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS) visible and infrared imagery; Context Camera (CTX) images; High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) images; Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) hyperspectral data; Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) topographic data; Mars Advanced Radar for Subsurface and Ionosphere Sounding (MARSIS) radar data; Monte Carlo subsurface models; thermal inertia modeling
abstract_note: The geologic history of the northern plains of Mars has been extensively debated. Speciﬁcally, the Vastitas Borealis Formation (VBF) represents an enigmatic surface unit that exhibits ﬂow morphologies at its boundary, extensive surface fracturing, tens of thousands of small mounds, and unique crater morphologies. Here we test the hypothesis that the VBF in the region of Chryse and Acidalia Planitiae, Mars, originated through the compaction and later expulsion of ﬂuid-laden sediments sourced from the shallow subsurface. We ﬁnd that the morphological, thermophysical, and spectral properties of the VBF marginal unit, in addition to the recent identiﬁcation of ﬁne-grained sedimentary layers in the shallow subsurface, are all consistent with such a formation mechanism. Estimates of volume loss based on “collar-like” morphologies present on high-standing buttes suggest that a minimum ﬂuid volume of ~13,500 km3 was expelled from the subsurface, making the VBF a signiﬁcant ancient hydrologic reservoir on the Martian surface. This formation mechanism lends additional insight into the sedimentary and aqueous history of the northern plains of Mars and unites morphologic, spectral, thermophysical, and structural observations under one consistent formation hypothesis.
research_content: This paper tests the hypothesis that the Vastitas Borealis Formation (VBF) in Chryse and Acidalia Planitiae formed through the compaction and expulsion of fluid-laden sediments from the shallow subsurface following outflow channel activity. The authors analyzed morphological, thermophysical, spectral, and geophysical data sets, including THEMIS, CTX, HiRISE imagery, CRISM hyperspectral data, MOLA topography, and MARSIS radar measurements. They identified thickening subsurface sedimentary units, surface deflation evidenced by perched collar morphologies on buttes, and thermophysical and spectral similarities between the VBF marginal unit, mud volcanoes, and subsurface sedimentary layers. Their findings support a formation mechanism involving deposition, burial, compaction, mud extrusion, and surface subsidence, implying massive volumes of water and sediment were involved in the northern plains' sedimentary history.

screening_result.reason: The paper tests hypotheses about the Vastitas Borealis Formation in Chryse Planitia involving fluid-laden sediment expulsion and identifies a significant ancient hydrologic reservoir, directly relevant to the question of an ancient ocean in the region.

paper_id: Small edifice features in Chryse Planitia, Mars_ Assessment of a mud volcano hypothesis.pdf
title: Small edifice features in Chryse Planitia, Mars: Assessment of a mud volcano hypothesis
authors: Komatsu, Goro; Okubo, Chris H.; Wray, James J.; Ojha, Lujendra; Cardinale, Marco; Murana, Alessio; Orosei, Roberto; Chan, Marjorie A.; Ormö, Jens; Gallagher, Ronnie
file_name: Small edifice features in Chryse Planitia, Mars_ Assessment of a mud volcano hypothesis.pdf
data_instruments_samples: HiRISE images and digital terrain models; CRISM VNIR and IR spectral data; SHARAD radargrams; THEMIS daytime infrared and visible images; CTX images
abstract_note: Small ediﬁce features that are less than a few kilometers in diameter and up to a few hundred meters in height are widely distributed in Chryse Planitia on Mars. They exhibit a broad range of morphological properties that are here classiﬁed as Type 1 (steep-sided cones typically with a summit crater), Type 2 (nearly ﬂat features with single or multiple central/summit craters or cones) and Type 3 (nearly circular features in plan view, characterized by steep sides and a broadly ﬂat summit area). Their origins have not been determined with certainty, but our study utilizing the High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) images supports the interpretation of mud volcanism, based on the observed morphological characteristics of these small ediﬁces and comparisons with terrestrial analogs. Additionally, hydrated minerals detected on these ediﬁce features in data from the Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM), further support the mud volcano hypothesis. Injection features such as clastic mega-pipes and sand blow features may coexist with the mud volcanoes. Alternative mechanisms such as magmatic volcanism are not excluded, but they have less support from our remote sensing observations. Further conﬁrmation or rejection of the mud volcano hypothesis will require in-situ investigation by landers or rovers.
research_content: This paper presents a detailed remote sensing study of small edifice features in Chryse Planitia, Mars, to assess the mud volcano hypothesis. The authors utilized high-resolution HiRISE images, CRISM spectral data, and SHARAD radar sounding to analyze morphological types, mineralogy, and subsurface structure of these features. They classified the small edifices into three types based on morphology and found nanophase ferric minerals and hydrated minerals on the edifices, supporting involvement of water. The SHARAD data showed no clear subsurface reflectors, suggesting a dry present-day subsurface. The study concludes that the small edifices are consistent with mud volcanism with some peculiarities unique to Mars, though alternative origins such as magmatic volcanism are not excluded.

screening_result.reason: The paper studies small edifice features in Chryse Planitia and supports a mud volcano hypothesis with hydrated minerals, which may relate to past water activity but does not directly address the existence of an ancient ocean.

paper_id: The Simud–Tiu Valles hydrologic system_ A multidisciplinary study of a possible site for future Mars on-site exploration.pdf
title: The Simud–Tiu Valles hydrologic system: A multidisciplinary study of a possible site for future Mars on-site exploration
authors: Pajola, Maurizio; Rossato, Sandro; Baratti, Emanuele; Mangili, Clara; Mancarella, Francesca; McBride, Karen; Coradini, Marcello
file_name: The Simud–Tiu Valles hydrologic system_ A multidisciplinary study of a possible site for future Mars on-site exploration.pdf
research_region: Simud Valles; Tiu Valles; Chryse Planitia
data_instruments_samples: Mars Global Surveyor MOLA DEM; Mars Express HRSC images and DEM; Mars Odyssey THEMIS visible images; Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX and HiRISE images; TES mineralogical maps; OMEGA hyperspectral data; CRISM multispectral and hyperspectral data; crater counting and size-frequency analysis; geological and geomorphological mapping; spectral parameter analysis for mineral identification
abstract_note: When looking for traces of past life on Mars, we have to look primarily for places where water was present, possibly for long time intervals. The Simud and Tiu Valles are two large outﬂow channels connected to the north with the Chryse Basin, Oxia Palus quadrangle. The area, carved by water during the Noachian/Early Hesperian is characterized by a complex geological evolution. The geomorphological analysis shows the presence of ﬂuvial and alluvial structures, interpreted as ﬂuvial channels and terraces, debris ﬂow fronts and short-lasting small water ﬂows coexisting with maar-diatremes and mud volcanoes. Several morphological features indicate a change in water ﬂux direction after the main erosive phase. During this period water originated from the Masursky crater and ﬂown southwards into the Hydraotes Chaos. This phenomenon caused the studied area to become a depocenter where ﬁnegrained material deposition took place, possibly in association with ponding water. This setting is potentially quite valuable as traces of life may have been preserved. The presence of water at various times over a period of about 1 Ga in the area is corroborated by mineralogical analyses of different areas that indicate the possible presence of hydrated minerals mixtures, such as sulfate-bearing deposits. Given the uniqueness of the evolution of this region, the long term interactions between ﬂuvial, volcanic, and tectonic processes and its extremely favorable landing parameters (elevation, slope, roughness, rock distribution, thermal inertia, albedo, etc.), we decided to propose this location as a possible landing site for the ESA ExoMars 2018, the NASA Mars 2020 and future on-site missions.
research_content: This paper presents a multidisciplinary study of the Simud–Tiu Valles hydrologic system on Mars, focusing on its geological evolution, geomorphology, mineralogy, and astrobiological potential. The authors used high-resolution digital elevation models, images, and spectral data from multiple Mars orbiters to reconstruct the history of water flow, sediment deposition, and volcanic activity in the area. They identified multiple evolutionary stages including catastrophic floods, debris flows, and a late phase of low-energy water fluxes, as well as maar-diatreme and mud volcano structures. Crater counting indicates deactivation of the system around 3.3 Ga. Mineralogical analyses using TES, OMEGA, and CRISM data suggest the presence of hydrated sulfate minerals and possible phyllosilicates. The site is proposed as a candidate landing area for future Mars missions due to its favorable engineering parameters and high potential for preserving biosignatures in sedimentary deposits.

screening_result.reason: This study focuses on the Simud and Tiu Valles outflow channels connected to Chryse Basin (part of Chryse Planitia), describing fluvial and alluvial structures and evidence of ponding water and hydrated minerals. Although it does not explicitly confirm an ancient ocean, it provides relevant geological and hydrological context about water activity in the Chryse Planitia region.

paper_id: The stratigraphy and history of Mars' northern lowlands through mineralogy of impact craters_ A comprehensive survey.pdf
title: The stratigraphy and history of Mars' northern lowlands through mineralogy of impact craters: A comprehensive survey
authors: Pan, Lu; Ehlmann, Bethany L.; Carter, John; Ernst, Carolyn M.
file_name: The stratigraphy and history of Mars' northern lowlands through mineralogy of impact craters_ A comprehensive survey.pdf
research_region: Mars northern lowlands; Chryse Planitia; Acidalia Planitia; Scandia region; Arcadia Planitia; Elysium Planitia; Utopia Planitia; Lyot vicinity
data_instruments_samples: CRISM L-detector targeted images (1.0–2.6 μm) from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter; CRISM S-detector data (0.4–1.0 μm) for select hydrated mineral detections; Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) topography data; Thermal Emission Spectrometer (TES) dust cover index; Mars global crater database; noise reduction and spectral parameter mapping algorithms; logistic regression and statistical tests
abstract_note: The basin-ﬁlling materials of the northern lowlands, which cover approximately one third of Mars’ surface, record the long-term evolution of Mars’ geology and climate. The buried stratigraphy was inferred through analyses of impact crater mineralogy, detected using data acquired by the Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars. Examining 1045 impact craters across the northern lowlands, we ﬁnd widespread olivine and pyroxene and diverse hydrated/hydroxylated minerals, including Fe/Mg smectite, chlorite, prehnite, and hydrated silica. The distribution of maﬁc minerals is consistent with inﬁlling volcanic materials across the entire lowlands (~1–4 × 107 km3), indicating a signiﬁcant volume of volatile release by volcanic outgassing. Hydrated/hydroxylated minerals are detected more frequently in large craters, consistent with the scenario that the hydrated minerals are being excavated from deep basement rocks, beneath 1–2 km thick maﬁc lava ﬂows or volcaniclastic materials. The prevalences of different types of hydrated minerals are similar to statistics from the southern highlands. No evidence of concentrated salt deposits has been found, which would indicate a long-lived global ocean. We also ﬁnd signiﬁcant geographical variations of local mineralogy and stratigraphy in different basins (geological provinces), independent of dust cover. For example, many hydrated and maﬁc minerals are newly discovered within the polar Scandia region (>60°N), and Chryse Planitia has more maﬁc mineral detections than other basins, possibly due to a previously unrecognized volcanic source. Plain Language Summary The northern lowlands of Mars (encompassing one third of the planet’s surface area) could have hosted a global ocean in the past. The lowlands are composed of several topographic depressions (“basins”) ﬁlled with sediments, which mask the nature of the underlying crust. Impact craters excavate up to several kilometers into the subsurface of the lowlands and expose the hidden record of its geologic history. Our comprehensive survey of the subsurface mineralogy excavated by these impact craters reveals widespread volcanic and hydrated silicate minerals. We did not ﬁnd widespread carbonate, chloride, or sulfate salts, which would have suggested a long-lived global ocean. However, our observations do suggest that impact craters have excavated a crust made of 1 to 2 km of volcanic material, which is on top of a water-altered basement containing hydrated silicate minerals. We have also discovered local variations in the different basins with evidence for new volcanic sources and for hydrated minerals in ancient crust near the north polar cap.
research_content: This paper presents a comprehensive survey of the mineralogy excavated by 1045 impact craters in Mars' northern lowlands using CRISM targeted spectral data. The authors applied an improved noise reduction algorithm to analyze CRISM L-detector images covering crater central peaks, walls, floors, and ejecta to identify mafic and hydrated minerals. They found widespread olivine and pyroxene indicating buried volcanic units with volumes greater than prior estimates, and diverse hydrated minerals including Fe/Mg smectites, chlorite/prehnite, and hydrated silica consistent with excavation of an aqueously altered ancient basement beneath 1–2 km thick mafic lava flows. Statistical analyses show that hydrated minerals are more frequently detected in larger craters, suggesting a deeper origin, and regional variations in mineralogy reveal local geological histories. No strong evidence was found for widespread carbonates or evaporative salts to support a global ocean hypothesis. The study constrains the subsurface stratigraphy of the northern lowlands, indicating a thick mafic volcanic layer overlying an altered basement and a surface layer with no distinct mineral signatures.

screening_result.reason: This paper directly addresses the northern lowlands of Mars including Chryse Planitia, analyzing mineralogy and stratigraphy related to water alteration and the lack of evidence for a long-lived global ocean, providing direct evidence relevant to the question of an ancient ocean in Chryse Planitia.

paper_id: The case against vast glaciation in Valles Marineris, Mars.pdf
title: The case against vast glaciation in Valles Marineris, Mars
authors: Kissick, Lucy E.; Carbonneau, Patrice E.
file_name: The case against vast glaciation in Valles Marineris, Mars.pdf
research_region: Valles Marineris; Candor Chasma; Chryse Planitia
data_instruments_samples: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE images; Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX images; Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) topographic data; morphological and slope profile analyses
abstract_note: The Valles Marineris of Mars form the largest system of interconnected canyons in the Solar System, where morphological, mineralogical, and structural evidence of widespread glaciation has been recently reported. However, neither precipitation models nor global water budgets can account for such a colossal fill, and the hypothesis has thus far remained unchallenged by additional scrutiny. Here, we present the first thorough case against a Valles Marineris glaciation by describing new evidence that precludes the existence of a glacier. Most crucially, we review High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) images of chaos terrain in Candor Chasma — previously interpreted as remnant glacial ice — and identify layered, boulder-rich scarps bearing no similarity to scarps of massive ice in Promethei Terra or the North Polar Layered Deposits. We also find no significant differences in the structure, morphology, and composition of chaos terrain in Candor and the Chryse Planitia region, which suggests Candor's Chaos, like Chryse's, is fractured highland terrain. We also review several other key supports for the glacial hypothesis, including the coincidence of an apparent glacial trimline with the water-bearing mineral jarosite, and the apparent presence of glacial features including kettle holes and sandur plains. These too are found to have more plausible explanations with non-glacial origins including tectonic reorganisation, groundwater sapping, and chaotic fracturing. We conclude that the Valles Marineris glacial hypothesis is inconsistent with both observed morphology and our understanding of the ancient Martian climate, and we find no evidence to support its existence.
research_content: This paper presents a detailed geomorphological study challenging the hypothesis of vast glaciation in Valles Marineris, Mars. The authors conducted a morphological analysis of chaos terrain in Central and East Candor Chasma, comparing it with chaos terrain in the circum-Chryse Planitia region, using high-resolution images from HiRISE and CTX. They examined features previously interpreted as glacial, such as chaos terrain, trimlines, kettle holes, outwash plains, and lateral moraines, and found them morphologically indistinguishable from fractured rock terrain formed by groundwater expulsion rather than ice. The study concludes that there is no morphological or mineralogical evidence supporting the existence of a vast glacier in Valles Marineris, and instead supports a groundwater origin for the chaotic terrain and associated features.

screening_result.reason: The paper discusses geological features in Chryse Planitia and nearby regions, challenging glaciation hypotheses and providing alternative explanations for terrain features, which offers useful context about water-related processes in the region relevant to ancient water presence.

paper_id: Hypotheses for the origin of the Hypanis fan-shaped deposit at the edge of the Chryse escarpment, Mars_ Is it a delta_.pdf
title: Hypotheses for the origin of the Hypanis fan-shaped deposit at the edge of the Chryse escarpment, Mars: Is it a delta?
authors: Adler, Jacob B.; Bell Iii, James F.; Fawdon, Peter; Davis, Joel; Warner, Nicholas H.; Sefton-Nash, Elliot; Harrison, Tanya N.
file_name: Hypotheses for the origin of the Hypanis fan-shaped deposit at the edge of the Chryse escarpment, Mars_ Is it a delta_.pdf
research_region: Chryse escarpment; Hypanis Valles; Xanthe Terra
data_instruments_samples: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE images and stereo DTMs; Mars Odyssey THEMIS thermal infrared images; Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX images and stereo DTMs; Mars Global Surveyor MOLA elevation data; Mars Express HRSC elevation data; CRISM Full-Resolution Targeted spectral cubes; JMARS software; ISIS software; Ames Stereo Pipeline; SOCET SET; LayerTools for ArcMap
abstract_note: We investigated the origin of the fan-shaped deposit at the end of Hypanis Valles that has previously been proposed as an ExoMars, Mars 2020, and human mission candidate landing site, and found evidence that the landform is an ancient delta. Previous work suggests that the deposit originated from a time of fluvial activity both distinct from and prior to catastrophic outflow, and crater counting placed the deposit’s age at ≥ 3.6 Ga. We found over 30 thin sedimentary strata in the proposed delta wall, and from our slope analysis conclude that the fluvial sequence is consistent with a lowering/retreating shoreline. We measured nearly horizontal bedding dip angles ranging from 0° to 2° over long stretches of cliff and bench exposures seen in HiRISE images and HiRISE stereo DTMs. From THEMIS night IR images we determined that the fan-shaped deposit has a low thermal inertia (150–240 Jm−2K−1s−1/2) and the surrounding darker-toned units correspond to thermal inertia values as high as 270–390 Jm−2K−1s−1/2. We interpret these findings to indicate that the fan-shaped deposit consists mostly of silt-sized and possibly finer grains, and that the extremely low grade and large lateral extent of these beds implies that the depositional environment was calm and relatively long-lived. Our assessment of the geomorphology and composition seems to indicate that the alluvial fan and mudflow hypotheses are less compatible. From our stratigraphic mapping we interpret the order of events which shaped the region. After the Chryse impact, sediment filled the basin, a confined lake or sea formed allowing a large delta to be deposited near its shoreline, the water level receded to the north, darker sedimentary/volcanic units covered the region and capped the light-toned deposit as hydro-volcanic eruptions shaped the interior of Lederberg crater, freeze/ thaw cycles and desiccation induced local fracturing, and finally wrinkle ridges associated with rounded cones warped the landscape following trends in degraded crater rims and existing tectonic features. The ancient deltaic deposit we observe today was largely untouched by subsequent catastrophic outflows, and its surface has been only moderately reshaped by over 3 billion years of aeolian erosion.
research_content: This paper investigates the origin of the Hypanis fan-shaped deposit at the edge of the Chryse escarpment on Mars to determine if it is an ancient delta. The authors analyzed high-resolution orbital images (HiRISE, CTX), stereo-derived digital elevation models (DTMs), thermal inertia data from THEMIS, and spectral data from CRISM. They performed geomorphological mapping, slope and dip angle measurements of sedimentary layers, thermal inertia and albedo analyses, and tested hypotheses distinguishing deltaic, mudflow, and alluvial fan origins. The results support a deltaic origin characterized by thin sedimentary strata with low dip angles, avulsion node migration, low thermal inertia consistent with fine-grained sediments, and geomorphology indicative of a subaqueous depositional environment, implying the presence of a large standing body of water in the Chryse basin during the late Noachian.

screening_result.reason: The paper investigates a fan-shaped deposit at the edge of the Chryse escarpment interpreted as an ancient delta formed in a confined lake or sea, providing direct geological evidence supporting the existence of an ancient standing body of water in the region.

title: Delta Deposits on Mars: A Global Perspective
authors: De Toffoli, B.; Plesa, A.‐C.; Hauber, E.; Breuer, D.
file_name: Delta Deposits on Mars_ A Global Perspective.pdf
research_region: Dichotomy boundary; Chryse Planitia; Acidalia Planitia; Memnonia; de Vaucouleurs Crater; Hypanis Valles
data_instruments_samples: Context Camera (CTX) global mosaic; Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) colorized elevation model; High Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) Digital Elevation Models; QGis software; crater size-frequency distribution analysis; impact crater statistics; global delta mapping and morphological classification
abstract_note: Deltas have long been considered a constraining element to reconstruct the water level of an ancient ocean that may have once occupied the northern lowlands of Mars, and recently this hypothesis started to be challenged. We investigate this hypothesis and present a global inventory of fan-shaped features showing typical deltaic traits across the entire Martian surface. For each element, we provide descriptive details and classifications based on morphology, location, and relation with characterizing environmental features. In this catalog of 161 deltas, we identified only six having high potential to constrain an oceanic paleoshoreline. Nonetheless, age and location of these candidates display discrepancies with what was previously suggested from independent data sets about shoreline age and locations. Our analyses hence indicate that deltas alone are insufficient to delineate a globally consistent ancient oceanic shoreline, but they have the potential to locally constrain the water level both in space and time.
research_content: This paper presents an updated global catalog of 161 delta deposits on Mars, including 68 newly identified features. The authors used geomorphological analysis of Context Camera (CTX) global mosaics and MOLA topographic data to classify deltas by morphology, basin type, and relation to water level changes. They identified 29 deltas located at the dichotomy boundary potentially related to a northern ocean margin, but only six deltas have high potential to constrain an oceanic paleoshoreline. Age and elevation analyses of these six deltas reveal discrepancies with previously proposed shoreline ages and locations, indicating that deltas alone cannot define a globally consistent ancient ocean water level on Mars. Instead, deltas likely record local-scale water level fluctuations and basin filling events.

screening_result.reason: This paper directly investigates delta deposits in Chryse Planitia and their implications for reconstructing ancient ocean shorelines on Mars, providing direct evidence and constraints relevant to the question of an ancient ocean in Chryse Planitia.

paper_id: Morphology, Morphometry and Distribution of Isolated Landforms in Southern Chryse Planitia, Mars.pdf
title: Morphology, Morphometry and Distribution of Isolated Landforms in Southern Chryse Planitia, Mars
authors: McNeil, Joseph D.; Fawdon, Peter; Balme, Matthew R.; Coe, Angela L.
file_name: Morphology, Morphometry and Distribution of Isolated Landforms in Southern Chryse Planitia, Mars.pdf
research_region: Southern Chryse Planitia; Oxia Planum; Mawrth Vallis
data_instruments_samples: Mars Orbital Laser Altimeter (MOLA) point data; High Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) digital terrain models; Context Camera (CTX) images; High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) images; Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS) nighttime infrared data; GIS analysis using ArcGIS; manual digitization of mound margins and prominences
abstract_note: The margin of Chryse Planitia, Mars, contains >105 kilometer-scale mesas, buttes, and plateaus (“mounds”), many of which are found in and around Oxia Planum, the ExoMars 2022 Rover landing site. Despite this, their origins and evolution are unknown. We have analyzed the morphologies and morphometries of 14,386 individual mounds to: (1) classify them based on their geomorphology; (2) constrain when they formed based on their stratigraphic and spatial relationships; and (3) develop hypotheses for their geological history. The mounds are classified as compound mounds, mesas, clustered mounds, and hills. Mound heights show that their elevations above the plains tend to a maximum height of 500 m. We interpret this as the thickness of a previously continuous layer that extended several hundred kilometers from the southern highlands into Chryse Planitia. Stratigraphy constrains the deposition of this layer to the Early-Middle Noachian, correlatable to the phyllosilicate-bearing strata of Mawrth Vallis, with similar layering also observable in some mounds, suggesting a genetic relationship. The mounds sometimes occur in circular arrangements, interpreted as an association with buried impact structures. We propose that the mounds formed through differential erosion after the premound layer was indurated by mineralization from groundwater in areas superposing underlying crustal weaknesses, for example, at buried crater margins. The subsequent differential erosion of this layer preferentially removed areas unaffected by this induration in the Late Noachian-Early Hesperian leaving the mound population seen at present. These features present accessible three-dimensional exposures of ancient layered rocks, and so are exciting targets for future study.
research_content: The authors systematically identified and classified 14,386 isolated mounds in southern Chryse Planitia into four morphological classes: hills, mesas, clustered mounds, and compound mounds. They measured mound morphometry using MOLA and HRSC elevation data, analyzed their spatial distribution, and examined stratigraphic relationships using CTX and HiRISE imagery. The study finds that the mounds are erosional remnants of a once-continuous, approximately 500 m thick Early to Middle Noachian layer, likely lithified and indurated by groundwater mineralization, with some mounds containing layering similar to the clay-bearing strata of Mawrth Vallis. The mounds predate the Late Noachian to Early Hesperian dark plains and are interpreted as preferentially preserved due to mineral cementation along crustal fractures and buried impact crater margins.

screening_result.reason: The paper analyzes isolated landforms in southern Chryse Planitia, interpreting their formation and stratigraphy related to ancient layered deposits and groundwater mineralization, which provides useful geological context for understanding past water activity in the region.

paper_id: Subsurface stratigraphy suggested by the layered ejecta craters in the Martian northern planitiae.pdf
title: Subsurface stratigraphy suggested by the layered ejecta craters in the Martian northern planitiae
authors: Gou, Sheng; Yue, Zongyu; Di, Kaichang; Pinet, Patrick C.; Bugiolacchi, Roberto; Niu, Shengli; Cai, Zhanchuan; Jin, Shuanggen
file_name: Subsurface stratigraphy suggested by the layered ejecta craters in the Martian northern planitiae.pdf
research_region: Acidalia Planitia; Chryse Planitia; Utopia Planitia; Isidis Planitia; Amazonis Planitia; Arcadia Planitia
data_instruments_samples: Robbins and Hynek (2012a) global crater database; Lagain et al. (2021) crater morphology database; THEMIS mosaic images (100 m/pixel); Context Camera (CTX) mosaic images (5 m/pixel); Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) topographic data; empirical excavation depth models; stratigraphic analysis methods
abstract_note: The formation of layered ejecta craters (LECs) is generally thought to be related to the subsurface water-ice. The distribution of LECs in the northern regions of Mars (0 to 70◦ N) features both local and latitudinal variations, e. g., there are generally few LECs within volcanic areas, and the observed minimum and median diameters of the LECs decreases with increasing latitude. The observed minimum diameters of the LECs in the six planitiae within the northern lowlands suggest the roof depth of the LECs-forming layer has clear lateral variability, ranging between ~90 m in the Arcadia Planitia and ~280 m in the Isidis Planitia. The observed LECs are suggested to mainly form during the Amazonian, implying that the LEC-forming water-ice-bearing strata might be still present. The variation might reflect the comprehensive influence on the subsurface water-ice by the climate conditions and geologic events during the Amazonian period. The proposed subsurface stratigraphies in the six planitiae suggest that the total thickness of the LECs-related strata in the Chryse Planitia is the largest (~4.6 km) and in the Arcadia Planitia is the smallest (~1.6 km). There could be as much as ~3.5–16 million km3 subsurface water stored in these strata, resulting in a ~24–110 m global equivalent layer (GEL) of water. Given that water is a fundamental ingredient to life, its migration from surface to subsurface shifts the focus of its exploration. Both Arcadia and Utopia Planitiae represent ideal candidates as locations where both shallow and deep subsurface water-ice might be abundant, they represent high-priority targets for future missions at mid-latitudes for biosignature searching and in-situ resource utilization.
research_content: This paper analyzes the distribution and characteristics of layered ejecta craters (LECs) in the northern Martian planitiae (0 to 70°N) to infer subsurface stratigraphy and water-ice content. The authors use global crater databases and THEMIS and CTX image data to estimate excavation depths of LECs, construct stratigraphic layers related to water-ice abundance, and estimate the volume of subsurface water-ice in six major planitiae. They find lateral variability in the roof depth of the LEC-forming water-ice-bearing layer, ranging from ~90 m in Arcadia Planitia to ~280 m in Isidis Planitia, and estimate total thicknesses of LEC-related strata from ~1.6 km to ~4.6 km. The study suggests that these strata may contain ~3.5 to 16 million km3 of subsurface water-ice, equivalent to a global water layer of ~24 to 110 m, and identifies Arcadia and Utopia Planitiae as high-priority targets for future exploration due to their abundant shallow and deep subsurface water-ice.

screening_result.reason: The paper discusses subsurface water-ice stratigraphy in Chryse Planitia, indicating significant subsurface water presence, which is relevant background information for understanding ancient water bodies but does not directly confirm an ancient ocean.

paper_id: Dichotomy retreat and aqueous alteration on Noachian Mars recorded in highland remnants.pdf
title: Dichotomy retreat and aqueous alteration on Noachian Mars recorded in highland remnants
authors: McNeil, Joseph D.; Fawdon, Peter; Balme, Matthew R.; Coe, Angela L.; Cuadros, Javier; Turner, Stuart M. R.
file_name: Dichotomy retreat and aqueous alteration on Noachian Mars recorded in highland remnants.pdf
data_instruments_samples: High Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) digital terrain models; Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) Precision Experiment Data Record; Context Camera (CTX) images; High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) images; Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) spectral cubes; Colour and Stereo Surface Imaging System (CaSSIS) images; MarsSI webGIS; United States Geological Survey (USGS) spectral library; spectral parameter analysis tools; zonal statistics and GIS analysis
abstract_note: Abstract The Mawrth Vallis region is a plateau situated on the highland side of Mars’ hemispheric dichotomy boundary. It has a >200-m-thick phyllosilicate-bearing stratigraphic succession that indicates extensive aqueous alteration between 4.1 Ga and 3.7 Ga, during the Noachian Period. In addition, thousands of kilometre-scale isolated mounds in the lowlands north and west of Mawrth Vallis have been identified. Here we use geomorphological and spectroscopic analyses to show that the mounds are erosional remnants that formed through retreat of the highland plateau in the Noachian. Consequently, the escarpment that marks the surface expression of the dichotomy must have receded south-southeast by hundreds of kilometres in this area. Lateral and stratigraphic geochemical variation in the mounds show that widespread, multiphase aqueous alteration occurred in situ across this region in surface and subsurface environments. The mound succession is underlain by a pyroxene-rich unit that represents unaltered material below the regional phyllosilicate-bearing sequence and is unconformably overlain by a thin capping unit that marks the end of large-scale regional aqueous activity. Thus, the mounds contain a stratigraphic record of the onset, evolution and cessation of Noachian aqueous conditions in this region, detailing the environment and climate of Mars at its most habitable.
research_content: This paper investigates the geomorphology, stratigraphy, and aqueous alteration history of isolated mounds and the highland plateau near Mawrth Vallis on Noachian Mars. The authors used high-resolution remote sensing data, including topographic transects and spectral analyses from CRISM, to demonstrate that the mounds are erosional remnants of a formerly contiguous phyllosilicate-bearing highland plateau that retreated hundreds of kilometers south-southeast. They identified stratigraphic units within the mounds recording a transition from unaltered pyroxene-rich basement to Fe/Mg-smectite-bearing altered strata and a thin capping unit marking the cessation of aqueous alteration. The study reveals multiphase aqueous alteration in surface and subsurface environments and documents large-scale dichotomy boundary retreat and landscape evolution during the Noachian.

screening_result.reason: The paper discusses aqueous alteration and geomorphological features in the Mawrth Vallis region and nearby lowlands including Chryse Planitia, indicating extensive water-related processes in the Noachian period. While it does not explicitly mention an ancient ocean in Chryse Planitia, the evidence of aqueous alteration and retreat of the highland plateau provides useful contextual information about water presence in the region.
